clues.q: Born Eunice Waymon, this singer-pianist recorded “Feeling Good” and “To Be Young, Gifted and Black.”
clues.hint: Nicknamed the “High Priestess of Soul.”

clues.q: This singer from Benin won Grammys for the albums “Celia” and “Mother Nature.”
clues.hint: Her early hits include “Agolo.”

clues.q: This pianist composed the jazz standard “’Round Midnight.”
clues.hint: A bebop pioneer known for his hats and angular melodies.

clues.q: Created by Lord Shorty in Trinidad and Tobago, this upbeat Carnival genre’s name blends “soul” and “calypso.”
clues.hint: A four-letter genre heard at every Caribbean Carnival.

clues.q: This saxophonist recorded the spiritual jazz suite “A Love Supreme” in 1964.
clues.hint: He also recorded the album “Giant Steps.”

clues.q: She created and starred in HBO’s “Insecure,” which premiered in 2016.
clues.hint: She first won fans with the web series “Awkward Black Girl.”

clues.q: In 2002, she became the first Black woman to win the Oscar for Best Actress, for “Monster’s Ball.”
clues.hint: She played Storm in the “X-Men” films.

clues.q: Which actress won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress for “12 Years a Slave”?
clues.hint: Kenyan-Mexican actress who later starred in “Us.”

clues.q: This director’s 1989 film “Do the Right Thing” takes place on one scorching day in Brooklyn.
clues.hint: His company is called 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks.

clues.q: Julie Dash’s 1991 film about Gullah women on the Sea Islands was the first feature by an African American woman to get a general US theatrical release.
clues.a: What is Daughters of the Dust?
clues.hint: Set off the Georgia and South Carolina coast in 1902.

clues.q: This 4th-century king of Aksum made Christianity his kingdom’s official faith.
clues.hint: His coins were among the first to show a cross.

clues.q: Visited by Ibn Battuta in 1331, this island city off Tanzania’s coast was a wealthy Swahili trading hub.
clues.hint: Its ruins include a Great Mosque and a palace called Husuni Kubwa.

clues.q: This Ethiopian king commissioned famous churches carved from solid rock, and a town now bears his name.
clues.hint: The churches date to around the 12th–13th centuries.

clues.q: A small golden rhinoceros was found in a royal grave of this Limpopo valley kingdom.
clues.hint: It flourished before Great Zimbabwe; now a South African national park.

clues.q: This Songhai ruler greatly expanded the empire and captured Timbuktu in 1468.
clues.hint: He was followed in power by Askia Muhammad.

clues.q: In 1975, he became the first Black man to win the Wimbledon men’s singles title.
clues.hint: The main stadium at the US Open is named for him.

clues.q: This 1967 Supreme Court case struck down state bans on interracial marriage.
clues.hint: The plaintiffs were Richard and Mildred.

clues.q: In 1966, this civil rights lawyer became the first African American woman appointed a federal judge.
clues.hint: She worked at the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.

clues.q: In 2001, he became the first African American US Secretary of State.
clues.hint: He had been Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

clues.q: In 1983, aboard the shuttle Challenger, he became the first African American in space.
clues.hint: An Air Force fighter pilot from Philadelphia.

clues.q: In 2021, this singer was named a National Hero of Barbados.
clues.hint: She founded the brand Fenty Beauty.

clues.q: Born into slavery, this general became the leading figure of the Haitian Revolution in the 1790s.
clues.hint: He died in a French prison in 1803.

clues.q: This Jamaican-born leader founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in 1914.
clues.hint: He also launched the Black Star Line shipping company.

clues.q: This poet from Martinique co-founded the Négritude movement with Léopold Senghor.
clues.hint: He wrote “Notebook of a Return to the Native Land.”

clues.q: This Trinidad-born historian wrote “The Black Jacobins” (1938), about the Haitian Revolution.
clues.a: Who is C. L. R. James?
clues.hint: He also wrote the cricket classic “Beyond a Boundary.”

clues.q: This 18th-century self-taught astronomer published almanacs and helped survey the boundaries of Washington, D.C.
clues.hint: He famously built a wooden clock in Maryland.

clues.q: In the 1940s, this surgeon developed large-scale blood-plasma storage and led the “Blood for Britain” project.
clues.hint: He taught surgery at Howard University.

clues.q: Cells taken from this woman in 1951 became HeLa, the first immortal human cell line.
clues.hint: Rebecca Skloot wrote a bestselling book about her life.

clues.q: In 1988, this ophthalmologist received a patent for the Laserphaco Probe for cataract surgery.
clues.hint: She co-founded an institute to prevent blindness.

clues.q: This surgeon founded Chicago’s Provident Hospital in 1891 and performed an early successful heart surgery there in 1893.
clues.hint: He later led Freedmen’s Hospital in Washington, D.C.

clues.q: Known as the “Godfather of Soul,” he recorded “I Got You (I Feel Good).”
clues.hint: Famous for his dramatic cape routine on stage.

clues.q: Known as the “Queen of Salsa,” this Cuban singer’s famous cry was “¡Azúcar!”
clues.hint: She sang with La Sonora Matancera.

clues.q: This Nigerian singer featured on Drake’s 2016 chart-topper “One Dance.”
clues.hint: His 2020 album was titled “Made in Lagos.”

clues.q: Called “The First Lady of Song,” this jazz singer was a master of scat.
clues.hint: She rose to fame singing with Chick Webb’s band.

clues.q: This Jamaican-born DJ is credited with launching hip-hop at a 1973 party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx.
clues.hint: He used two turntables to stretch out the breakbeat.

clues.q: Queen Latifah played magazine editor Khadijah James in this 1990s Fox sitcom.
clues.hint: Four friends shared a Brooklyn brownstone.

clues.q: Anthony Anderson and Tracee Ellis Ross starred in this ABC family sitcom that premiered in 2014.
clues.hint: The family’s last name was Johnson.

clues.q: This writer-director won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay for the 2017 horror film “Get Out.”
clues.hint: He is half of a sketch duo with Keegan-Michael Key.

clues.q: For “Gone with the Wind,” she became the first African American to win an Academy Award.
clues.hint: She won Best Supporting Actress in 1940.

clues.q: In 1964, this Bahamian-American actor became the first Black man to win Best Actor, for “Lilies of the Field.”
clues.hint: He also starred in “In the Heat of the Night.”

clues.q: This Malian city’s Great Mosque, rebuilt in 1907, is re-plastered with mud in a yearly festival.
clues.hint: It sits on a floodplain near the Niger River.

clues.q: Ruled by the Alaafin, this Yoruba state was famed for its cavalry in the 1600s and 1700s.
clues.hint: Its namesake town is in southwestern Nigeria.

clues.q: Celebrated in an epic told by griots, this founder of the Mali Empire won the Battle of Kirina.
clues.hint: Known as the “Lion King” of Mali.

clues.q: Tradition says a Golden Stool descended from the sky to unite this West African kingdom.
clues.hint: Its capital was Kumasi, in today’s Ghana.

clues.q: Famous bronze plaques were made for the royal palace of this West African kingdom, ruled by an Oba, in present-day Nigeria.
clues.a: What is the Kingdom of Benin?
clues.hint: Its capital lies in today’s Edo State.

clues.q: In 1960, at age six, she integrated William Frantz Elementary School in New Orleans.
clues.hint: Norman Rockwell painted her walk to school.

clues.q: Signed by Lyndon Johnson in 1965, this law outlawed discriminatory voting practices such as literacy tests.
clues.a: What is the Voting Rights Act?
clues.hint: It came one year after the Civil Rights Act.

clues.q: In 1972, this Houston lawyer became the first Black woman from the South elected to the US House.
clues.hint: Famous for her powerful voice and 1976 convention keynote.

clues.q: Elected in 1989, he became Virginia’s governor and the first elected Black governor of a US state.
clues.hint: A Richmond native and Korean War veteran.

clues.q: In 1950, this diplomat became the first African American to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
clues.hint: He worked for the United Nations.

clues.q: Once known for the graffiti tag “SAMO,” this Brooklyn-born painter became a 1980s art star.
clues.hint: He collaborated with Andy Warhol.

clues.q: This artist painted Barack Obama’s official portrait for the National Portrait Gallery, unveiled in 2018.
clues.hint: He often places subjects against vivid floral backgrounds.

clues.q: Which artist painted the 60-panel “Migration Series” in 1940–41?
clues.hint: He grew up in Harlem and was in his early twenties.

clues.q: In 2018, the founder of Off-White became artistic director of Louis Vuitton menswear.
clues.hint: He trained as an architect and worked with Kanye West.

clues.q: This Harlem Renaissance sculptor created “The Harp” for the 1939 New York World’s Fair.
clues.hint: She ran an influential art school in Harlem.

clues.q: This Southern dish of black-eyed peas and rice is traditionally eaten on New Year’s Day.
clues.hint: Said to bring good luck in the coming year.

clues.q: Thickened with roux and often okra or filé, this stew is a Louisiana staple.
clues.hint: Usually served over rice in New Orleans.

clues.q: This tomato-based one-pot rice dish is the subject of a friendly rivalry between Nigeria and Ghana.
clues.hint: Cooked with peppers, onions and spices; party favorite.

clues.q: Jamaica’s national dish pairs saltfish with this fruit, which looks like scrambled eggs when cooked.
clues.hint: It originally came to the Caribbean from West Africa.

clues.q: Called the “Queen of Creole Cuisine,” this chef ran her family’s celebrated restaurant in the Tremé neighborhood of New Orleans for decades.
clues.hint: She inspired Disney’s Princess Tiana.
